query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a combined friction stir processing (FSP) and optimized solution heat treatment to a W–Cu composite will modify the interfacial microstructure, reducing phase separation and eliminating interfacial voids, thereby enhancing thermal conductivity under joint operational (heat-transfer and irradiation) conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A W–Cu composite featuring W particles or interconnected W ligaments dispersed in a Cu matrix that exhibits phase separation and interfacial voids which limit thermal transport.
generation.intervention: Subject the composite to friction stir processing (FSP) followed by a controlled solution heat treatment at a temperature sufficiently high to promote interfacial diffusion without melting the constituents (analogous to ~525 °C used in similar composites) for an optimized duration.
generation.conditions: Processing in solid state at parameters similar to those used for achieving a graded interfacial structure; testing under simulated heat-transfer loads and irradiation conditions relevant to plasma-facing/cooling joint environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A newly engineered graded interphase or core–shell interfacial layer formed during the FSP and subsequent heat treatment.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced atomic diffusion at the W–Cu interface during heat treatment promotes a gradual compositional transition, reducing thermal expansion mismatch and eliminating void formation. This improved metallurgical bonding facilitates more continuous phonon and electron pathways, thus boosting thermal conductivity.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated composite will exhibit a statistically significant improvement in thermal conductivity compared to the untreated composite, due to the reduction in interfacial defects and enhanced diffusion-bonded interfaces.
generation.baseline: The untreated W–Cu composite which suffers from phase separation and interfacial voids that lower its effective thermal conductivity under operating conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to W–Cu composites processed via FSP with subsequent heat treatment at controlled temperatures (below melting points) and tested under heat-transfer loads and irradiation levels relevant to plasma-facing and cooling joint applications. It may not hold if the composite geometry or processing parameters fall outside these optimized ranges.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal heat treatment time and precise processing parameters for the W–Cu system are not yet established and may require further refinement. The magnitude of thermal conductivity improvement is also uncertain until experimentally verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite samples: one set processed via standard manufacturing (untreated) and another processed with FSP followed by an optimized solution heat treatment. Subject both sets to identical heat-transfer and irradiation conditions in a controlled laboratory setup. Measure and compare their thermal conductivities using standardized methods such as laser flash analysis and in situ thermal imaging.
measurements: Phase distribution and interfacial integrity (EDS mapping or XRD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the FSP and heat-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in thermal conductivity (beyond measurement uncertainty) compared to the untreated composite, or if post-treatment microstructural analyses reveal persistent phase separation and voids, then the hypothesis is falsified.

First, a straight groove with a length of 90 mm, a width of 2 mm, and a depth of 4 mm was machined at the middle of each workpiece plate (Figure 1a). The HEA particles were filled into the groove and pressed tightly. Secondly, a pinless rotating tool was adopted to cap the surface of the groove to avoid the spattering of reinforcement particles in the next step (Figure 1b). Finally, a three-pass FSP was carried out in the same direction along centerline of the preprocessed weld to disperse the HEA particles (Figure 1c). The pin tool for FSP was made by H13 hardened steel with a shoulder diameter of 20 mm, a pin diameter of 10 mm with a right thread, and a pen length of 4.5 mm. The parameters of rotating speed, travel speed, plunged depth, and tilting angle were 1200 rpm, 20 mm/min, 0.2 mm, and 2°, respectively. In this context, one of the biggest challenges is the development of structural and functional materials that can withstand the conditions inside the reactor: high temperature, high heat flux, and intense flux of high energy neutrons []. The diverter, located at the bottom of the plasma chamber, where the thermal power from the plasma is exhausted [], is one of the most challenging areas. Tungsten (W), with a high melting temperature, low sputtering rates, low neutron activation, and low tritium and deuterium retention [,], was chosen as the plasma-facing material. CuCrZr alloy was chosen as the heat sink due to its high thermal conductivity and strength. However, there is a gap between the operating temperatures of these two materials. Tungsten presents a high ductile–brittle temperature transition (DBTT) [], which requires a high-temperature operation, while CuCrZr alloy presents relatively low working temperatures (180–350 °C) [], with loss of ductility caused by irradiation embrittlement at lower temperatures and loss of mechanical strength at higher temperatures due to over-aging [,]. Nuclear fusion-based power reactors require advancements with regard to high-temperature and plasma-facing materials in order to prevent degradation due to the exposure to high-temperature and high-energy neutron flux produced during deuterium-tritium fusion reactions. The severity of the service environment is expected to increase in upcoming fusion reactors with increased power ratings and those under transient scenarios. For instance, the heat load on the divertor, a key component of the tokamak design, , is expected to increase to 10 MW/m2 (steady state) and 20 MW/m2 (transient for 10 seconds). The inner and outer vertical targets of the divertor, where the kinetic energy of plasma particles is converted into heat, must withstand loads up to ~7–40 MJ/m2 and ~4–25 MJ/m2, respectively, under plasma disruption, . Therefore, unprecedented thermal, mechanical and physical characteristics are required for fusion reactor materials.
